name: Paper Folding and Punching — Predicting the Unfolded Pattern
whatIsIt: A square paper is folded one or more times, then a hole is punched through all the folded layers. Your job is to predict exactly how many holes — and where — will appear once the paper is fully unfolded again, based on how many times it was folded and where the punch landed.
whyNeeded: This builds mental visualization of layered symmetry: understanding that a punch through folded layers creates a MIRRORED pattern across every fold line once unfolded — real spatial reasoning used in design, packaging, and geometry.
realLifeUses: Reasoning sections of SSC, banking and railway exams
Paper crafts, origami, and pattern cutting (like paper snowflakes)
Understanding symmetry in packaging and textile design

vocabulary.meaning: The line along which the paper is folded — every hole gets mirrored across each crease when unfolded.
A hole made through all the currently-folded layers of paper at once.
How the paper looks once every fold is opened back out flat, showing all the mirrored holes.

story.title: The Paper Snowflake Rule
story.text: Zoya's teacher folds a square paper in half once (one crease) and punches a single hole near the edge, away from the fold. 'How many holes when I unfold it?' she asks. Zoya thinks: one fold means the hole gets mirrored across that one crease line — so 2 holes total. She's right! Then the teacher folds a fresh paper twice (two creases, a plus-sign) and punches once. 'Now how many?' Two fold lines means the hole mirrors across BOTH — 4 holes total, one in each quarter of the paper.
story.extractedProblem: A paper folded once (1 crease) is punched once, away from the fold. How many holes appear unfolded? What about a paper folded twice (2 creases) punched once, away from both folds?
story.answerInStory: 1 fold → 2 holes. 2 folds → 4 holes — each fold line doubles the hole count, as long as the punch isn't exactly on a crease.

visual.caption: One fold line means the punch mirrors across that single crease — resulting in exactly 2 holes once unfolded.

teachingGallery.title: Two fold lines double the mirroring
teachingGallery.note: With two creases (a horizontal AND a vertical fold), a single punch mirrors across BOTH lines — appearing once in each of the paper's four quarters.

examples.caption: Two fold lines (crossing like a plus sign) mirror one punch into all four quarters — 4 holes total, one per quarter.

standardMethod.summary: Count the number of fold lines (creases). If the punch is NOT exactly on any crease, the number of holes when unfolded is 2 raised to the power of the number of fold lines (2 for 1 fold, 4 for 2 folds). If the punch IS exactly on a crease, that mirror direction doesn't create a new hole, so the count is less than the usual power of 2.
steps: Count how many fold lines (creases) the paper has.
Check whether the punch location lies exactly on any crease line, or is clearly off every crease.
If off every crease: holes when unfolded = 2 to the power of (number of fold lines).
If exactly on one crease: that fold direction doesn't double the hole, so divide the usual count by 2 for each crease the punch sits on.
Positions mirror symmetrically across every crease — sketch each mirrored copy to find exact hole positions, not just the count.

alternateMethods.name: Unfold one step at a time
alternateMethods.whenToUse: When multiple folds make the direct formula confusing.
steps: Mentally unfold just the LAST fold made — this doubles the current hole(s), mirrored across that last crease.
Repeat for the second-to-last fold, then the first — doubling again each time.
This step-by-step approach avoids errors even in more complex multi-fold problems.
alternateMethods.example: 2 folds, 1 punch: unfold the last crease → 2 holes. Unfold the first crease → 4 holes total.

workedExamples.problem: A square paper is folded once (1 crease) and punched once, clearly away from the fold line. How many holes appear when unfolded?
steps: Count the fold lines: 1.
Check the punch: it's away from the crease, not on it.
Holes when unfolded = 2 to the power of 1 = 2.
The unfolded paper shows 2 holes, mirrored across the single crease.

workedExamples.problem: A square paper is folded twice (2 creases, like a plus sign) and punched once, clearly away from both fold lines. How many holes appear when unfolded?
steps: Count the fold lines: 2.
Check the punch: away from both creases.
Holes when unfolded = 2 to the power of 2 = 4.
The unfolded paper shows 4 holes, one mirrored into each quarter.

workedExamples.problem: A square paper is folded once (1 crease) and punched exactly ON the crease line. How many holes appear when unfolded?
steps: Count the fold lines: 1, so the usual formula gives 2 to the power of 1 = 2.
But the punch is exactly ON the crease — mirroring a point that's already on the fold line lands it right back on itself.
So instead of 2 separate holes, there is only 1 hole, sitting right on where the crease was.
The unfolded paper shows just 1 hole.

trickPractice.intro: Off-crease punches double per fold line; on-crease punches break that doubling.

questions.q: 3 fold lines, punch clearly off every crease. How many holes when unfolded?
If the punch lands exactly on a crease, does that crease still double the hole count?

options.label: No — mirroring a point on the line lands back on itself

questions.answer: No — mirroring a point on the line lands back on itself
hintLadder: A point on the fold line has no 'other side'.
Mirroring it gives the same point.
No extra hole from that crease.

questions.q: 2 fold lines, punch clearly off both creases. How many holes when unfolded?

commonMistakes.mistake: Always applying the 2-to-the-power formula even when the punch is exactly on a fold line, missing that on-crease punches don't double.
commonMistakes.fix: Always check the punch's exact location first. Only apply the full 2-to-the-power formula when the punch is clearly off every crease line.

commonMistakes.mistake: Miscounting how many distinct crease lines the paper ends up with (e.g. treating a diagonal fold and its reverse as two separate creases when they're the same line).
commonMistakes.fix: Carefully trace and count only the DISTINCT crease lines visible if you flattened the paper back out — don't count a fold made and then unfolded again as a real crease.

commonMistakes.mistake: Mirroring a hole in the wrong direction (e.g. reflecting across a horizontal crease as if it were vertical).
commonMistakes.fix: Each crease has its own mirror direction — a vertical crease reflects left-right; a horizontal crease reflects top-bottom. Match the mirror direction to the actual crease orientation.

easy.q: 1 fold line, punch off the crease. How many holes when unfolded?
2 fold lines, punch off both creases. How many holes when unfolded?
Does an 'on-crease' punch usually give MORE or FEWER holes than the standard formula predicts?
hintLadder: The crease's mirror doesn't add a new copy.
So the total is less than 2-to-the-power.

medium.q: 3 fold lines, punch off every crease. How many holes when unfolded?
2 fold lines, punch exactly on ONE of the two creases (but off the other). How many holes when unfolded?
hintLadder: One crease doesn't double (punch is on it), so divide by 2.

medium.q: A paper is folded, unfolded, then folded again along the SAME line. How many distinct creases does it actually have?
hintLadder: Refolding the same line doesn't create a new crease.
It's still just one physical fold line.

challenge.q: 1 fold line, punch exactly on the crease. How many holes when unfolded?
4 fold lines, punch off every crease. How many holes when unfolded?
2 fold lines, punch exactly on BOTH creases (right at the center where they cross). How many holes when unfolded?
hintLadder: Both mirror directions land back on the same center point.
Neither crease adds a new copy.

questions.q: 1 fold line, punch off the crease. Holes when unfolded?
2 fold lines, punch off both creases. Holes when unfolded?
3 fold lines, punch off every crease. Holes when unfolded?
Does punching exactly on a crease line still double the hole count for that fold?
hintLadder: A point on the line mirrors to itself.

questions.q: 1 fold line, punch exactly on the crease. Holes when unfolded?
hintLadder: Normally 2, but on-crease breaks the doubling.

teachBackPrompt: Teach a friend the 2-to-the-power rule for paper folding, using the 2-fold, 4-hole example, and explain why an on-crease punch breaks the doubling.

revisionCard.summary: Count the distinct fold lines. If the punch is clearly off every crease, holes when unfolded = 2 to the power of the number of fold lines (2, 4, 8...). If the punch sits exactly on a crease, that fold direction doesn't double the hole count — divide by 2 for each crease it sits on. Each hole mirrors symmetrically across its crease's direction (vertical crease = left-right mirror; horizontal crease = top-bottom mirror).

gameMission.title: The Jungle Leaf-Punch Puzzle
gameMission.brief: Fold and punch jungle leaves, then predict exactly how many holes appear when they're unfolded!

realLifeProject: Fold a real square paper once or twice, punch a hole away from the creases, predict the hole count using the formula, then unfold it and check if your prediction was correct.

rememberIt.unpack: Each fold line doubles the hole count, unless the punch sits exactly on that crease.

studentQuestions.q: What if the paper is folded diagonally instead of straight up-down or left-right?
studentQuestions.a: The same rule applies — the mirror direction just follows the diagonal crease instead of a straight horizontal or vertical line. Count the fold lines and check on-crease vs off-crease exactly the same way.

Each fold line independently doubles whatever holes already exist by mirroring them across it — one fold doubles once (×2), two folds double twice (×2×2=×4), and so on, which is exactly how powers of 2 build up.
